title: Your first model call in 5 minutes
summary: Learn the five building blocks of Azure AI Gateway, create a gateway with a Microsoft Foundry model in the portal, the Azure CLI, or Bicep with azd, and make your first model call, all in about five minutes with nothing to clone.

text: Azure AI Gateway gives your apps and agents one governed endpoint for models and tools. In five minutes you create a gateway, put a Microsoft Foundry model behind it, and call that model the way an app does: with the gateway's URL, an alias in the model field, and a runtime API key. Click through the AI Gateway portal, paste a few Azure CLI commands into Azure Cloud Shell, or deploy a Bicep template with one azd up . There's nothing to clone or install. Set up once, in the portal, in Cloud Shell, or with azd up. Then every call goes through the gateway: it checks the key, routes the alias, and signs in to Foundry with its own identity. # Before you begin You need an Azure subscription where you can create resources and role assignments, for example Owner , or Contributor plus Role Based Access Control Administrator . The gateway gets a role on your Foundry account, so that it can call the model with its own identity. Each track lists the tools that it needs at its start. # How it works Every call that goes through AI Gateway uses the same five building blocks. In this quick start you create one of each. Building block What it does In this quick start Gateway The Azure resource ( Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways ) that gives your apps one runtime URL for models and tools Your gateway, at https://<gateway>.<location>-01.ai.gateway.azure.com Model provider A connection to a backend. The gateway signs in to it with its own managed identity, so your apps never hold a backend key Your Foundry account. The Azure CLI and Bicep tracks name the provider foundry-models Model A backend deployment that the gateway can route to The Foundry deployment gpt-6-luna Alias The name that apps send in the model field. title: How Azure AI Gateway works
summary: A 20-minute visual tour of the AI Gateway tier of Azure API Management. Follow one request through the gateway, meet models, aliases, MCP servers, policies, and identities, and pick the learning path that fits your role.
text: Every team that ships generative AI hits the same questions. Which models may we call, and with which keys? Who spent the tokens? How do we stop one agent from starving everyone else, or from calling a tool it should never touch? The AI Gateway tier of Azure API Management answers them in one place: apps and agents call one gateway, and the gateway decides who gets in, which model or tool answers, what each call may cost, and what gets recorded. Narrated walkthrough: how Azure AI Gateway works (3 min) Apps, agents, and coding agents call one gateway. The gateway authenticates them, applies policies, routes model calls through aliases, federates tools, and emits OpenTelemetry. Note The AI Gateway tier is in public preview in East US 2 and Sweden Central . The gateway itself is free during the preview. Connected services, such as Microsoft Foundry inference and Application Insights, are billed normally. # Before you begin This lab is a guided reading. You don't need to deploy anything. If you already have a gateway, open the AI Gateway portal ↗ in another tab and follow the portal tour at the end. If you don't have one yet, read on. You create your first gateway in Provision your first AI gateway . # How it works The gateway sits on the path of every model call and every tool call. It has two faces: Data plane : the runtime endpoints your code calls, at https://<gateway>.eastus2-01.ai.gateway.azure.com . Control plane : the product portal at ai.gateway.azure.com ↗ and the Azure Resource Manager API for the Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways resource type, which you call with az rest , Bicep, or any REST client. Building block What it is Example Gateway An AI Gateway resource ( Microsoft.ApiManagement/aigateways ) in your subscription https://<gateway>.eastus2-01.ai.gateway.azure.com Backend model A model at a provider, such as a Foundry deployment or an Anthropic model gpt-6-luna at Microsoft Foundry Alias The stable, gateway-wide name clients send in the model field chat MCP server One governed MCP endpoint that federates tools from one or more sources /default/toolservers/<server-name>/mcp Policy A rule on the gateway or on one asset: limits, budgets, safety, filters Token rate limit, Cost limit Access How callers authenticate: API keys or Microsoft Entra ID roles api-key header or Entra token Managed identity How the gateway authenticates to backends Foundry User role on the Foundry account Monitoring OpenTelemetry metrics, logs, and traces for every call Application Insights or any OTLP endpoint Model calls use protocols developers already know. The OpenAI-compatible base URL is https://<gateway-host>/default/models/openai/v1 (append /responses or /chat/completions ), and Anthropic Messages lives at /default/models/anthropic/v1/messages . The gateway passes requests through without translating between OpenAI and Anthropic formats, so call each model on an interface it advertises. # Follow one request Press Play to send a request through the gateway. Then switch scenarios to see where each policy stops a request and which status code the caller gets back. Every applicable policy is evaluated before the gateway forwards a request. If one blocks it, the backend is never called. Three rules explain almost every response you'll see in these labs: Policies run before the backend. If any applicable policy blocks a request, the gateway answers right away and never calls the backend. Each block has a predictable status. 401 for missing or invalid credentials, 403 for IP filters and cost limits ( LlmCostQuotaExceeded ), 429 with Retry-After for token and request rate limits, and 400 for content safety. Everything is recorded. Allowed and blocked calls both show up in Monitoring , along with the policies that affected them. # Models and aliases A backend model is what a provider serves. An alias is what your clients call. Microsoft Foundry imports create an alias for each model by default, and you can add more. Because clients only know the alias, you can move it to a newer or cheaper model without a code change, and the alias keeps its own policies. Two aliases can share one backend model with different policies. Retargeting an alias needs no client change. You can put models from Microsoft Foundry, Azure OpenAI, OpenAI, Anthropic, AWS Bedrock, Google Vertex AI, and custom OpenAI-compatible endpoints behind aliases. You try it in Route models from several providers behind aliases . # MCP servers and tools Agents need tools as much as models. An MCP server on the gateway gives agents one endpoint and one credential for tools from remote MCP servers, OpenAPI specifications, built-in connectors, and Foundry Toolbox. Tool names are namespaced per source, and tool availability decides which tools clients can see and call. One MCP endpoint federates tools from several sources. Tool availability and policies apply to every call. # Policies and scopes You add a policy at gateway scope , where it applies to every compatible asset including assets you add later, or to individual assets : a backend model, an alias, or an MCP server. Pick an asset below to see every policy that applies to it. Policy Applies to When it blocks Token rate limit Models and aliases 429 with Retry-After Request rate limit Models, aliases, and MCP servers 429 with Retry-After Cost limit Models and aliases 403 LlmCostQuotaExceeded Content safety Models, aliases, and MCP servers 400 IP filter Models, aliases, and MCP servers 403 Agent 365 tool threat protection MCP servers Denies the tool call At gateway scope, the policy type decides which assets are relevant. A gateway-scope cost limit, for example, tracks one budget across all models. # Identities on both sides The gateway separates who is calling from how the gateway reaches the backend . Callers use an API key or a Microsoft Entra token with one of the AI Gateway data-plane roles. The gateway uses its own managed identity, or a provider key it stores, to call backends. Callers

text: The first product team wants to use gpt-6-luna , which already runs in your Microsoft Foundry account. You don't want to hand every team the Foundry endpoint and a provider key. In this lab you publish the deployment through your gateway, give the team a runtime API key of its own, and make the first call from the playground, a shell, and code. The gateway authenticates to Foundry with its own managed identity, so the app never sees a Foundry credential. The gateway checks the caller's key, applies policies, calls the backend with its own identity, and records telemetry on the way back. # Before you begin Complete Provision your AI Gateway . You don't want either team to hold an Anthropic key, and you don't want to edit their code every time you switch models. title: Route an alias across models by priority and weight
summary: Put two Foundry models behind one alias, canary a new model version with an 80/20 weighted split, then prefer one model by priority, all without changing the model name that clients send.
text: Your team wants to try gpt-6.1-sol , but every app already sends "model": "chat" , and nobody wants a big-bang switch. In this lab you put the current model and the new one behind the same alias, send a fifth of the traffic to the new model, count where the requests land, and then use priority to choose which model is preferred. The apps never change the model name they send. Priority picks the tier. Weight splits the traffic inside it. # Before you begin Complete Publish a Foundry model and make your first call . You need the gateway, a runtime API key, and the gpt-6-luna backend model. Lab 02 also gave the gateway the Foundry User role on your Foundry account, which covers the new deployment in this lab. Permission to change the gateway, for example Contributor on its resource group, and to create deployments in the Foundry account. The Azure CLI ↗ 2.75 or later, signed in with az login . The Bash commands also use jq ; the PowerShell commands need PowerShell 7 or later. Optional: Publish models from any provider behind stable aliases explains aliases in more depth. Set these variables once. Every track and the Verify section reuse them. Bash PowerShell Copy The CLI and Bicep tracks of lab 02 name the provider foundry-models . A portal import names it after your Foundry account. To check, list the providers and the models of each one: Bash PowerShell Copy Deploy the candidate model in the same Foundry account as gpt-6-luna . Pick a region where the model is available. Model inference is billed per use. Bash PowerShell Copy # How it works An alias holds a list of backend models. Each one has a priority and a weight: Setting Values Default What it does Priority Whole number from 0 to 100 0 Lower numbers are preferred. Requests go to the backend models with the lowest priority number. Weight Whole number from 1 to 100 1 Splits traffic among the backend models that share a priority, in proportion to their weights. A backend model's Share within priority is its weight divided by the sum of the weights at its priority. Weights 80 and 20 give 80% and 20%; weights 3 and 1 give 75% and 25%. text: Chat apps and agents stream their replies: the model sends text a few tokens at a time, so people start reading after a second or two instead of waiting for the whole answer. In this lab you stream through the gateway with curl, PowerShell, and the OpenAI SDKs, read every event the client receives, and then prove that a token limit still counts every streamed token. Token and cost limits are checked before the stream starts. While the stream flows back, the gateway records its token usage for limits, budgets, and Monitoring. # Before you begin Complete Publish a Foundry model and make your first call . The body is a series of server-sent events (SSE): each one is a data: line with a JSON chunk, followed by a blank line. The gateway passes each chunk on as the model produces it, and the response carries x-accel-buffering: no , which tells proxies such as NGINX not to hold it back. A token limit or cost limit is checked before the gateway forwards the request. When a counter is exhausted, the client gets an ordinary JSON error, such as 429 with Retry-After , and no stream starts. text: Your gateway now serves several apps from one model deployment. One batch job sends long prompts in a tight loop and eats the deployment's tokens-per-minute (TPM) capacity, so every other app starts to fail. In this lab you give each caller its own token allowance at the gateway, so a noisy neighbor gets a 429 with Retry-After and everyone else keeps working. Each caller identity gets its own token counter. When a counter is exhausted, the gateway answers 429 without calling the backend. # Before you begin Complete Publish a Foundry model and make your first call . You need a gateway, an imported model, a callable alias, and a runtime API key from Access › Keys . For the CLI, REST, and IaC tracks: the Azure CLI ↗ 2.75 or later, signed in with az login , plus jq for the Bash snippets. The CLI track calls the Azure Resource Manager REST API with az rest , because the az aigateway extension doesn't manage the new aigateways resource type yet. Permission to change the gateway, for example Contributor on the resource group. Set these variables once. Every track and the Verify section reuse them. Bash PowerShell Copy Tip Not sure which alias your clients call? Open the model in Models and check its Aliases tab. The value in the request model field must match an alias exactly. # How it works A token limit is a policy that the gateway evaluates before it forwards a request. It keeps a counter of the tokens that each caller consumed in the current window. While the counter is under the limit, the request goes through and the tokens in the response are added to the counter. When the counter reaches the limit, the gateway answers 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header and never calls the backend. In this lab you set that up as a cost limit at the gateway, so a caller who runs out of budget is stopped before the model is called. A cost limit attached to a model budgets spend on that model. Attached at gateway scope, it tracks one budget per caller across all models. # Before you begin Complete Throttle tokens per caller with token limits . text: Your agents call tools that read web pages, tickets, and documents, and any of that content can carry a prompt injection or leak sensitive data back to the model. Content filters on the model don't see what goes into a tool or what comes out of it. In this lab you add Agent 365 tool threat protection to an MCP server, so Microsoft Defender and Microsoft Purview evaluate each tool request, each tool result, or both, and the gateway only lets allowed calls through. The gateway asks for an allow decision before the tool runs, after it returns, or both. Anything other than an allow fails closed. # Before you begin Complete Federate MCP tools behind one endpoint . This lab protects the learn MCP server from that lab. Any MCP server in your gateway works. Complete Go keyless with Microsoft Entra ID and RBAC . Tool threat protection only works for callers that send a delegated Microsoft Entra ID bearer token issued for AI Gateway. A Microsoft Defender or Microsoft Purview license in your tenant. Permission to manage policies on the gateway, for example Contributor on its resource group, and permission to create role assignments if your user doesn't have a data-plane role yet. The Azure CLI ↗ 2.75 or later, signed in with az login as a user (not a service principal). The CLI snippets call the Azure Resource Manager REST API with az rest , because the az aigateway extension doesn't manage the new aigateways resource type yet. For the test scripts and the Bash snippets: curl and jq (Bash) or PowerShell 7 or later. Note Agent 365 tool threat protection is an emerging capability of the AI Gateway tier preview, which is available in East US 2 and Sweden Central. Labels and behavior can change; see the release note ↗ . AI Gateway itself is free during the preview; Defender and Purview are licensed separately. Set these variables once. The steps and the Verify section reuse them. Bash PowerShell Copy # How it works Tool threat protection is a policy on one MCP server. It covers every tool on that server, whether the server is backed by remote MCP endpoints, OpenAPI services, or both, and every caller. The gateway first runs its usual authentication, authorization, and policies. Only requests that pass are sent for evaluation. For each tools/call , the gateway exchanges the caller's delegated token on behalf of the user (OBO) and asks Microsoft Defender and Microsoft Purview for a verdict on malicious content, prompt injection, and sensitive-data risks. Discovery and session traffic, such as initialize , tools/list , and notifications, isn't evaluated. The evaluation must return a valid allow . A denial, timeout, token-exchange failure, malformed verdict, or unavailable evaluator fails closed: the caller gets a normal tool result over HTTP 200 with isError: true , a denial code, and a correlation ID. Stage What's evaluated What it prevents Cost Before tool invocation The tool name and arguments The tool never runs, so there are no side effects One evaluation round trip After tool invocation The tool result, including error results The result never reaches the agent. The tool already ran . One evaluation round trip Both Both of the above Requires two allow decisions Up to two round trips per call # Prepare a delegated caller The policy evaluates each call on behalf of the signed-in user, so you test it with your own user token. Give your user permission to call tools on the server, then make one call before you add the policy.
